Twenty-one GB2SM participated in this photovoice study taking photographs to depict and discuss their previous suicidality. Data were collected from in-depth individual interviews in which participants discussed their photographs and in turn ofered verbal/narrative accounts of suicidality.

The study used a photovoice methodology, an approach grounded in the traditions of community-based and participatory action research where individuals afected by an issue take and narrate photographs to describe their experiences and perspectives (Wang, 1999). This method was selected as suicide is highly stigmatized (Sudak, Maxim, & Carpenter, 2008), and photovoice can increase the feasibility of studying stigma ridden issues because it allows participants to discuss their experiences bypassing sole reliance on words (Olife & Bottorf, 2007; Wang, 1999). Following university ethics approval, participants were recruited through the distribution of posters within Vancouver's gay village and online via social media sites. The ads invited potential participants to contact the study team by email or telephone. Participants were eligible if they (1) had previous experiences of suicidality, (2) were at least 19 years old, (3) self-identifed as a gay, bisexual or two-spirit man, and (4) spoke English. Men who self-disclosed current suicidality were excluded from the study and referred to mental health services.

First, adverse childhood events and negative adolescent experiences were described as the root causes of mental health struggles and suicidality. Second, violence and homophobia had disrupted these men's education and employment opportunities and some participants detailed how their lack of capital and challenges for maintaining employment shaped their suicidality. Third, a sociality of stigma and sense of isolation compounded experiences of suicidality.

Participants were asked to take photographs to illustrate their previous experiences of suicidality, including what they believed caused and/or triggered their suicide thoughts, the strategies they used to manage their suicidality, and their perspectives on GB2SM's suicide.

[/page/2/Text/8] A multi-stage thematic analysis approach (Braun & Clark, 2006) was used to identify GB2SM's perspectives on suicidality within a nexus of constraints and opportunities for optimal mental health. First, the interview transcripts were imported to Nvivotm 11.0, and the frst two authors read all the transcripts multiple times to get familiar with the data, writing memos to note initial interpretations and trends, and to create a provisional codebook. Then, the frst author performed an initial round of coding. At this stage, descriptive labels and codes were further developed to organize data segments, and the analyses of data allocated to each code were reviewed to inductively derive key themes. The initial codes included gender, negative early experiences, migration, homophobia, employment, poverty, social isolation, culture, violence, and health care.

evidence.section_title: Violent and Challenging Starts: "I Did Not  Have a Childhood. My Life Has Been Really Full  of Garbage"
evidence.quote: The participants' experiences of adverse childhood events and violence were strongly represented as contributors to their suicidality and refected inequities in relations of power. The participants detailed many forms of abuse at the hands of people in positions of power, such as parents and older family members across their life-course; however, violence featured in the participants' narratives of their childhood and adolescence. For many, these violent and challenging starts to life were described as the root cause of many of their adult life difculties, including their mental health struggles and suicidality.

evidence.section_title: Spiraling Down Without Capital: "I Couldn't See  a Future"
evidence.quote: Men's lack of capital, defned in this study as under-employment, unemployment and fnancial struggles, was described as a critical factor in the suicidality by many participants. ... These challenges added to early childhood and adolescence traumas, which profoundly afected their lifecourse trajectory. ... For several participants, fnancial difculties were strongly connected to their suicidality. ... failing in his responsibility to be the “breadwinner” and not being able to provide for his family heightened his depression and diminished his self-worth ... These quotations provide evidence of how career losses or failures to launch weighed heavily on men already disadvantaged by their minority sexual identity, gender expression and/or mental illness. ... For some participants, the experience of “spiraling down” was spurred by an ended romantic relationship. ... The interconnections between class, income and suicidality were described as circular to some extent. As Raymond, a 60-year-old gay man, summated, “people are depressed because they are poor, they stay poor because they are depressed.” ... Finally, lack of fnancial capital was described by some participants as a barrier to their recovery from depression and suicidality.

evidence.section_title: Lack of Belonging and Isolation: "I Have Spent  a Long Time Feeling Lonely and Alone"
evidence.quote: Feelings of not belonging and of isolation repeatedly appeared in the participants' narratives and refected power relations. While the participants described diverse circumstances across their life-course that led them to feel isolated, the cumulative toll of these challenges heightened their risk for suicidality.

The current study ofers novel insights about the interplaying dynamics of suicidality among a diverse group of GB2SM. Echoing the fndings of other research (D'Augelli & Grossman, 2001; Diaz et al., 2001; Ferlatte et al., 2015; Irwin et al., 2014; Paget et al., 2016; Plöderl et al., 2013, 2014; Salway et al., 2018), the participants' narratives were replete with descriptions of adverse childhood events including abuse and violence, which they linked to their suicidality. These challenges were deeply enmeshed with other critical moments across their histories and were often manifested in the 'spiraling down without capital' and eventual 'social isolation' key themes in the analysis. In describing their struggles over identity, upbringing, personhood, place as well as sexuality, the participants revealed the ways in which 'risk factors' are a product of multiple aspects of the person, and fundamentally challenge sexuality as the 'catch all' determinant of suicidality among GB2SM. This is not to diminish the centrality of sexual identity and homophobia in the production of sufering and suicidality. Rather, the fndings outlined in this article suggest a view of suicidality as complex and produced by multiple and intertwined factors and forms of domination (including homophobia, classism, sexism, racism, mental health stigma), rather than the outcome of a singular and independent factor. Building on this, the importance of considering the lifecourse of GB2SM in suicide research was evident whereby long-standing struggles and difculties that predated adulthood featured prominently in the narratives of participants. The life-course dimension of suicidality refects the importance of embedding seemingly disparate 'events' related to suicidality within a broader process of becoming—rather than being—'suicidal' (Blackman, 2012). In essence, formative moments and normative infuences haunted (Gordon, 2008) the participants and often assembled in highly problematic ways to tip them in the direction of suicide. That is, not only is suicidality uniquely multifactorial, but it is also temporally bound. A focus on the process of becoming thereby reveals suicidality as inextricably linked in a historicity of intersecting factors. Such dynamics refect many of the logics espoused previously in work on intersectionality, but that have hitherto not been incorporate in suicidality work. The current fndings also highlight the particular ways in which limits or losses of fnancial capital contribute to suicidality among GB2SM. Indeed, other studies have found that a disproportionate number of sexual minorities are living in poverty (Lee Badgett, Durso, & Schneebaum, 2013; Ross et al., 2016). In conclusion, suicidality among GB2SM is the result of a constellation of factors beyond sexuality. After all, GB2SM are also 'classed,' 'gendered' and 'raced,', and as such, they are vulnerable to other forms of structural violence including classism, sexism and racism.
